input: Representative sampling of a gas emission is concerned with obtaining a sample whose composition genuinely reflects the composition of the emission as a whole, and there are several aspects of the sampling procedure that have to be got right if this goal is to be achieved. The first of these aspects is the location at which samples are taken: the sample should be drawn from a point in the duct or stack where the gas is thoroughly mixed and where the stream is representative of the whole flow, rather than from a stagnant corner or from a position immediately downstream of a disturbance, where the composition may be quite untypical. The second aspect is the way in which the sample itself is built up: rather than relying on a single portion of gas, a proper sample is formed from a number of separate increments, each of them taken at a different time and combined together, so that the final sample averages over the fluctuations that occur in the emission. This brings us to the reason why a single grab sample can be so misleading: the composition of an emission is not constant, but varies with the state of the process, with the load on the plant and with time, and a grab sample captures nothing more than the state of the emission at one particular instant. Any limits that the sampling is intended to check against are a separate matter, since regulatory limits of that kind belong to the permit held by the site and not to the sampling method itself.
target: Representative sampling of a gas emission takes a portion of the gas whose composition stands for the composition of the whole emission over the period the sample is meant to cover. Where samples are taken decides much of the result. The sampling point is placed where the gas in the duct is mixed across the section and the stream at the point is the stream as a whole, not at a stagnant edge and not in the disturbed flow behind a bend or an obstruction, where the local composition can differ from the mean. How the sample is formed matters as much as where it is taken. One sample is built from several increments, each increment drawn at a different time across the sampling period and the increments combined, so the sample carries the average of the emission over that period rather than the state of the emission at a single moment. A single grab sample misleads for that reason. The composition of an emission varies with the state of the process that produces it, with load and with time, and a portion drawn at one instant freezes one state of a moving quantity: the same duct sampled at another moment returns another composition, and neither portion alone is the emission. The increments are the correction, since their spread across the period is what makes the combined sample representative. Numerical limits play no part in the method: the limits against which a result is judged belong to the permit held by the site, and the passage states none.
